lead: Air blown over a wet surface dries it faster than still air. The vapour still crosses the layer next to the surface by diffusion, but moving air sweeps the vapour away and keeps that layer thin and its gradient steep. One number, the convective mass transfer coefficient k<sub>c</sub>, captures how well a flowing fluid carries a species to or from a surface, with no film thickness needed. Absorbers, cooling towers and dryers are sized with it.
prereq: You need Fick's first law, molar flux and the steady diffusion result for a stagnant film, from the topic of molecular diffusion and diffusivity.

sections.h3: The coefficient replaces a film thickness

blocks.text: For a stagnant film, molecular diffusion gave N<sub>A</sub> = D<sub>AB</sub>(C<sub>A1</sub> − C<sub>A2</sub>)/δ, where D<sub>AB</sub> is diffusivity (m²/s) and δ is film thickness (m). In a flowing fluid no fixed δ exists. The layer next to the surface is thin at the leading edge, grows downstream and breaks into eddies in turbulent flow. So δ cannot be measured, and the formula cannot be used as it stands.

blocks.where: N<sub>A</sub> is the molar flux of A across the interface, mol/(m²·s); C<sub>Ai</sub> is the concentration of A just at the interface, mol/m³; C<sub>A∞</sub> is the concentration of A in the well-mixed bulk fluid, mol/m³; k<sub>c</sub> is the convective mass transfer coefficient, m/s.

blocks.text: The unit follows: mol/(m²·s) divided by mol/m³ gives m/s. So k<sub>c</sub> looks like a velocity, but it is not the speed of the fluid. It is the molar flux per unit concentration difference. It is a transport coefficient, not a speed.

All the unknown fluid mechanics — film thickness, turbulence, surface shape — is pushed inside kc. Theory cannot give kc from first principles for most equipment. It is measured, or predicted from correlations kc = (DAB/L) × f(Re, Sc). Those groups and correlations are in Chapter 2.3.

sections.h3: Gas and liquid forms, local and average

blocks.text: For a gas, partial pressure is the natural driving force. With p<sub>A</sub> = C<sub>A</sub>RT, where p<sub>A</sub> is partial pressure (atm), R is the gas constant and T is absolute temperature (K), the flux law is N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>G</sub>(p<sub>Ai</sub> − p<sub>A∞</sub>). Comparing forms gives k<sub>G</sub> = k<sub>c</sub>/(RT). With R in m³·atm/(kmol·K), k<sub>G</sub> comes out in kmol/(m²·s·atm). The liquid-side coefficient k<sub>L</sub> uses liquid concentrations and has units of m/s.

The coefficients come in two types, because the flux formula for molecular diffusion differs with what B does. For A diffusing through stagnant B (N<sub>B</sub> = 0, as when water evaporates into air), a film of thickness z gives N<sub>A</sub> = D<sub>AB</sub> P (p<sub>A1</sub> − p<sub>A2</sub>)/(R T z p<sub>Bm</sub>), so k<sub>G</sub> = D<sub>AB</sub> P/(R T z p<sub>Bm</sub>). For equimolar counter-diffusion (N<sub>A</sub> = −N<sub>B</sub>, as in distillation) the film gives k′<sub>G</sub> = D<sub>AB</sub>/(R T z) with no p<sub>Bm</sub>. The two are linked by k<sub>G</sub> p<sub>Bm</sub> = k′<sub>G</sub> P, and in mole fractions by k<sub>y</sub> y<sub>Bm</sub> = k′<sub>y</sub>. A correlation measured at low flux gives the primed value; for diffusion through stagnant B divide it by y<sub>Bm</sub>, the log mean of the B mole fractions at the two ends of the film.

A local coefficient applies at one point and varies with position because the boundary layer changes. An average coefficient applies over the whole surface: total molar flow equals average coefficient × total area × mean driving force. Design uses averages. A gas-side coefficient belongs to the gas film, a liquid-side coefficient to the liquid film. When both matter they combine into an overall coefficient, as Chapter 2.2 shows.

sections.h3: Boundary layer, turbulence and the size of k<sub>c</sub>

blocks.text: Air flows over a flat plate. A concentration boundary layer of thickness δ<sub>c</sub> (m) builds up, inside which concentration falls from C<sub>Ai</sub> at the wall to C<sub>A∞</sub> outside. The wall flux is N<sub>A</sub> = −D<sub>AB</sub>(∂C<sub>A</sub>/∂y) at y = 0, where y is normal to the plate. A thin layer holds a steep gradient, so flux and k<sub>c</sub> are large.

The layer thickens roughly as √x from the leading edge. The wall gradient weakens, so local k<sub>c</sub> falls with distance. The average over a plate of length L is larger than the trailing-edge local value because the leading part transfers well. Hence the average is the honest number for a whole surface.

In turbulent flow, eddies add an eddy diffusivity far larger than the molecular one, so bulk transport is fast. That is why gas velocity strongly affects kc. A thin laminar sublayer always survives at the wall, and species cross it by molecular diffusion. That sublayer is the bottleneck, so kc rises with velocity but never without limit. This picture leads to film and surface-renewal theories in Chapter 2.4.
So coefficients are sorted three ways: by position (local or average), by combination (individual film or overall) and by driving force, which also fixes the phase and the unit.

figure.caption: The worked example. Water vapour falls from the saturated value 1.42 mol/m³ at the surface to 0.426 mol/m³ in the 30 % humidity air. The real profile is curved; film theory replaces it by a straight line with the same slope at the wall, which reaches the bulk value at δ = D<sub>AB</sub>/k<sub>c</sub> = 1.3 mm. The flux is 1.99×10⁻² mol/(m²·s), or 2.03×10⁻² after the stagnant-air correction.

A panel lists k_c 0.020 m/s, driving force 0.994, flux 1.99e-2 mol per square metre per second, 1.29 kg per square metre per hour, and 2.03e-2 after the correction.

examples.question: Air at 300 K and 1 atm (101.325 kPa) with 30 % relative humidity flows over a water surface, also at 300 K. The vapour pressure of water at 300 K is 3.54 kPa. The gas-side coefficient, measured at low flux, is k′<sub>c</sub> = 0.020 m/s. Find the evaporation flux in mol/(m²·s) and kg/(m²·h), find k<sub>G</sub> and k<sub>y</sub>, and correct for diffusion through stagnant air.
steps: Interface: the gas just above the water is saturated, p<sub>Ai</sub> = 3.54 kPa, so C<sub>Ai</sub> = p<sub>Ai</sub>/(RT) = 3540/(8.314 × 300) = 1.42 mol/m³.
Bulk: 30 % relative humidity gives p<sub>A∞</sub> = 0.30 × 3.54 = 1.06 kPa and C<sub>A∞</sub> = 0.30 × 1.419 = 0.426 mol/m³.
In mass per hour: 1.99×10⁻² × 0.018 kg/mol × 3600 s/h = 1.29 kg/(m²·h). The flux runs from the surface into the air, so water evaporates.

Gas-phase forms: k<sub>G</sub> = k<sub>c</sub>/(RT) = 0.020/(8.314 × 300) = 8.02×10⁻⁶ mol/(m²·s·Pa) = 0.812 mol/(m²·s·atm), and k<sub>y</sub> = k<sub>G</sub> P = 0.812 mol/(m²·s). Check: y<sub>Ai</sub> − y<sub>A∞</sub> = (3.54 − 1.06)/101.3 = 0.0245, and 0.812 × 0.0245 = 1.99×10⁻² mol/(m²·s), the same flux.

Stagnant air: p<sub>B1</sub> = 101.33 − 3.54 = 97.79 kPa at the surface and p<sub>B2</sub> = 101.33 − 1.06 = 100.27 kPa in the bulk, so p<sub>Bm</sub> = (100.27 − 97.79)/ln(100.27/97.79) = 99.02 kPa and P/p<sub>Bm</sub> = 1.023.
examples.answer: N<sub>A</sub> ≈ 2.0×10⁻² mol/(m²·s), about 1.3 kg of water per m² per hour; k<sub>G</sub> = 8.0×10⁻⁶ mol/(m²·s·Pa) and k<sub>y</sub> = 0.81 mol/(m²·s). The stagnant-air correction is only 2.3 % here, because water vapour is dilute in the air.

traps: Matching coefficient to driving force. k<sub>G</sub> needs a partial pressure difference in atm; k<sub>c</sub> needs a concentration difference in mol/m³.
Forgetting k<sub>c</sub> is per unit interfacial area. In a packed tower the measured group is often k<sub>c</sub>·a, where a is area per m³, with units 1/s.
Using the other phase's bulk concentration instead of the interface value. The interface is set by equilibrium (Chapter 2.6).
Comparing kG and kL directly. Their driving forces differ; convert both to one overall coefficient based on one phase (Chapter 2.2).

quiz.q: Define the convective mass transfer coefficient and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: It is k<sub>c</sub> in N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>c</sub>(C<sub>Ai</sub> − C<sub>A∞</sub>), the molar flux per unit concentration difference. Its SI unit is m/s.

quiz.q: Why do we use k<sub>c</sub> instead of the stagnant-film thickness δ when the fluid is moving?
quiz.a: In moving fluid there is no fixed film. The layer is thin at the leading edge, grows downstream and is broken by turbulence, so δ cannot be measured or predicted. That unknown behaviour is lumped into k<sub>c</sub>, which is measured or taken from a correlation.

quiz.q: Convert k<sub>c</sub> = 0.02 m/s at 300 K and 1 atm into k<sub>G</sub>. Take RT = 0.0246 m³·atm/mol.
quiz.a: k<sub>G</sub> = k<sub>c</sub>/RT = 0.02 ÷ 0.0246 = 0.81 mol/(m²·s·atm) = 8.1 × 10⁻⁴ kmol/(m²·s·atm). Unit check: (m/s) ÷ (m³·atm/mol) = mol/(m²·s·atm). With R = 0.08206 m³·atm/(kmol·K), RT = 24.6 m³·atm/kmol and k<sub>G</sub> = 0.02/24.6 = 8.1 × 10⁻⁴ kmol/(m²·s·atm).

quiz.q: Along a flat plate in laminar flow the local k<sub>c</sub> falls with distance x, yet the average coefficient over length L is greater than the local value at x = L. Explain both facts.
quiz.a: The boundary layer thickens roughly as √x, so the wall gradient weakens and local k<sub>c</sub> falls. The average is weighted over the whole plate; high local values near the leading edge pull it above the trailing-edge value.

quiz.q: A student has k<sub>G</sub> = 2 × 10⁻⁵ kmol/(m²·s·atm) and a concentration difference of 0.40 mol/m³, and reports N<sub>A</sub> = 8 × 10⁻⁶ mol/(m²·s). Identify the error and give the correct method.
quiz.a: The student multiplied a partial-pressure coefficient by a concentration difference, so the units do not match. Convert first: at 300 K, k<sub>c</sub> = k<sub>G</sub> RT = 2×10⁻⁵ × 0.08206 × 300 = 4.92×10⁻⁴ m/s (R in m³·atm/(kmol·K)). Then N<sub>A</sub> = 4.92×10⁻⁴ × 0.40 = 1.97×10⁻⁴ mol/(m²·s), about 25 times the reported value. Or use k<sub>G</sub> with a partial-pressure difference in atm.

beyond: Not for the exam. In a packed column the measured group is often k<sub>c</sub> a, because the wetted area a inside random packing is hard to measure on its own. CFD now computes local k<sub>c</sub> on catalyst surfaces and in microchannels. Search terms: volumetric mass transfer coefficient, concentration boundary layer, F-type mass transfer coefficient.
